text: His confession was thrown out by the Supreme Court of the United States. He went back to prison anyway.
Phoenix, 1963. Ernesto Miranda is taken into a room and questioned. He confesses. Nobody had told him he could stay silent. Nobody had told him he could have a lawyer.
His case climbed all the way up. In 1966, by five votes to four, the Court agreed. That confession should never have counted.
So the state tried him again. A new trial, on other evidence. Convicted a second time. The most famous name in American law belongs to a man who was still found guilty.
He never won his freedom. He won something that outlived him. Why the rule survived when he did not: the full case is on the channel.
